raw_response:
I’m keeping it mostly the way that has fed my family before. On my 7 mu, I won’t gamble too much. Wheat and maize are still my main steady crops because if wheat does alright, at least I have grain and some cash, and maize follows right after so the land doesn’t sit empty. But I still want a bit of cotton because when the price is decent, it helps with household expenses. Since some family members work outside, I can’t make a plan that needs too much hand labor or too many extra trips. Water from the well is available, but pumping costs money, so I will save irrigation for the key stages. For fertilizer, I usually follow what worked on my own fields and what the extension people said, but I still do a bit more if I worry the crop may go weak. I’d rather spend a little more than see the field turn yellow and lose yield.

For the 7 mu, I’ll put 5 mu into wheat-maize double cropping and 2 mu into cotton. Wheat will be sown in early October with a local improved wheat seed. I’ll put base fertilizer before sowing, then topdress once around jointing if the seedlings look a bit pale. I’ll irrigate about 3 times if the season is normal: once after sowing if moisture is short, once at jointing, and once at grain filling if needed. After wheat harvest in early June, I’ll move fast and plant summer maize on the same 5 mu within a few days, with minimum tillage because the turnaround is tight and labor is limited. For maize, I’ll use hybrid seed, put most fertilizer at planting, and maybe one more small topdress around the big bell stage. Irrigation for maize depends on rain, but usually 1 time is enough unless summer is too dry. For the 2 mu cotton, I’ll plant in late April. Cotton needs more watching, especially for insects, so I won’t expand it too much. I’ll use moderate fertilizer, 2 irrigations if needed, and expect more labor there because of pest checks and picking.
